questions.question: Eleanor, you've said the opening gives us two narrators running at different temperatures — the ironic observer and Miss Matty the memoirist. Can you just walk us through what you mean by that? Because I think most people come to this novel thinking it has one voice.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to lay out her dual-narrator thesis clearly as the segment's opening framework, establishing the structural stakes before the others complicate them

questions.question: James, Eleanor's framing makes the novel sound almost experimental — two voices in productive tension. But you've been reading this more materially. When you hit that first line — 'Cranford is in possession of the Amazons' — are you hearing a formal experiment, or are you hearing Gaskell describing a specific legal and economic situation?
questions.intent: Set up the disagreement between formal/structural reading and materialist reading; get James to quote c2:p0 and make the property-ownership argument

questions.question: Caroline, you've called the 'Amazons' framing deceptive — and I suspect you'd push back on both of them here. Because James is saying these women have real power through property, and Eleanor is saying the narrative structure itself creates a kind of ironic distance. You're saying something darker, aren't you — that the language is doing the ideological work?
questions.intent: Draw out Caroline's 'entrapment disguised as charm' thesis and get her to quote the 'elegant economy' line; position her as complicating both James's materialism and Eleanor's formalism

questions.question: James, let's go to the moment everyone agrees is the emotional centre — c12:p41, Miss Matty's reflection on how different her life turned out from what she expected, and that tear that drops on the narrator's hand. You've said that tear is the sound of someone who remembers thinking she had choices. But Eleanor and Caroline are going to say something about memory and language there too — so before they do, what exactly do you hear in that passage?
questions.intent: Get James to quote 'only so very different to what I expected' and make the argument about structural constraint and loss; prime Eleanor and Caroline to respond with their competing readings

questions.question: Eleanor — last word on this, because I want to put James's reading directly to you. He's saying Miss Matty's tears are about genuine deprivation, about foreclosed choices under coverture and economic constraint. You've suggested the novel is doing something more structural with memory — that it's not just sadness, it's about the gap between who we thought we'd be and who we became. Are those the same thing, or are you actually disagreeing with him?
questions.intent: Force Eleanor to either concede to or directly contest James's materialist reading of c12:p41; create a moment of genuine intellectual friction rather than polite agreement

steering_notes: This segment should move from the formal/structural question (Eleanor's dual-narrator thesis) through the materialist challenge (James on property and law) to the darkest reading (Caroline on complicity and entrapment) — and then land on c12:p41 as the passage that tests all three frameworks simultaneously. Don't let anyone treat 'elegant economy' as simply charming — push back if needed. The goal is to establish early that this is a novel with teeth, so the rest of the episode has somewhere to go.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor frames the dual-narrator structure; James immediately grounds it in material reality — those two readings aren't necessarily opposed but the guests may treat them as if they are, which is productive

Caroline and James both hear darkness in 'elegant economy' but for different reasons: James sees rationalized injustice, Caroline sees the reader being made complicit. Put those two readings side by side explicitly

Eleanor thinks Caroline's reading of c12:p41 as nostalgic sadness flattens the structural move Gaskell is making; Caroline thinks Eleanor's structural reading undersells the emotional knife. That's a genuine disagreement worth surfacing
All three want to quote 'only so very different to what I expected' — use that convergence to ask whether they're actually reading the same line differently or talking past each other

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that I haven't been able to shake — that Gaskell *refuses* to let this death become literary. What do you mean by that? Because on paper, this is a perfect Victorian tearjerker: noble man, dying daughters, railway villain. Why doesn't it feel like one?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to articulate her core argument about anti-climactic detail and Gaskell's refusal of melodrama — sets up the Pickwick passage and the 'helplessness' quote early

questions.question: Eleanor, you've mapped out how Gaskell tells this death *three times* — the news, the eyewitness account, the newspaper. Can you walk us through that? Because you said something about each version stripping something human away, and I want to hear that argument out loud.
questions.intent: Draw out Eleanor's structural argument about the three iterations of Brown's death — gets her to read the dialect eyewitness passage aloud from c3:p51 and sets up the contrast between grief and public narrative

questions.question: James, I want to put something to you directly. Both Caroline and Eleanor are treating Captain Brown's death as this profound, carefully crafted literary moment. You seem to want to say — hang on, this is actually a *political* event. A man died because Victorian England had no safety net. Am I hearing that right?
questions.intent: Force James to make his social-document argument against the grain of the literary readings — provoke the disagreement about whether this is tragedy-of-fate vs tragedy-of-exposure, and get him to read Jenny's 'nasty cruel railroads' line

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to bring you back on something James just said — because I think you actually disagree about Miss Jenkyns's moment of moral panic, that 'God pardon me if ever I have spoken contemptuously' line. James reads that as guilt, not wisdom, and says the structural injustice gets swallowed by sentiment. What do you say to that?
questions.intent: Set up direct disagreement between Eleanor and James over whether Jenkyns's self-recrimination is meaningful moral transformation or Gaskell letting the social system off the hook

questions.question: Caroline, let's end on the passage you most wanted to read — that 'there was that in the room' moment from c3:p71. Eleanor loves it too, but I suspect you love it for different reasons. Read it for us, and tell me why Gaskell could have failed completely here and somehow didn't.
questions.intent: Close the segment with the novel's most powerful death passage read aloud — surface the difference between Caroline's emotional reading and Eleanor's structural one, and give the segment a resonant ending

steering_notes: The big tension to keep live throughout: is this death *literary* (Caroline, Eleanor) or *political* (James)? Don't let either camp settle too comfortably — push Caroline and Eleanor on whether beautiful prose about grief is itself a kind of sentimentality Gaskell is supposedly resisting, and push James on whether the social critique lands *because* of the emotional machinery, not in spite of it. The Pickwick detail is the pivot point all three agree on but read completely differently — return to it if the conversation stalls. Keep energy up by naming the contradiction: Gaskell is supposed to be refusing melodrama, but she's also giving us one of the most affecting deaths in Victorian fiction. How does that work?
cross_engagement_targets: James argues Jenny's 'nasty cruel railroads' is working-class fury at a system — Caroline thinks it's personal love, not philosophy. Get them to fight this out directly: can it be both, and does it matter?

Eleanor reads Miss Jessie's consolation speech in c3:p77 as structurally controlled spiritual work; Caroline reads it as emotional honesty mastered by will; James reads it as what you say when the law offers nothing. These are three genuinely different readings of the same sentence — surface this explicitly.

Both Caroline and Eleanor resist reading Brown's death as heroic martyrdom; James is the one most likely to frame it in terms of class exposure rather than heroism. But all three risk the same thing: making it *mean* something, when Caroline's strongest argument is that Gaskell refuses meaning. Push on this.

questions.question: James, you've said the comedy in Cranford is basically doing ideological work — making oppressive social codes feel warm and cosy when they're actually keeping these women trapped. But that's a pretty dark reading of what most people experience as a genuinely funny, affectionate book. Sell me on it. What's the line that makes you feel Gaskell knows exactly what she's doing?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to read or paraphrase the 'We none of us spoke of money' passage and the Spartans line — and to commit to the strongest version of his thesis before the others push back

questions.question: Caroline, I suspect you want to argue with basically everything James just said. Because you've described the Spartans line — same line he just quoted — as evidence that Gaskell finds these women *heroic*. How can the same sentence be doing such completely different things for both of you?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation over c2:p16 — get Caroline to read 'they were like the Spartans, and concealed their smart under a smiling face' and make the case that the simile is sympathetic rather than damning; expose the crux of the disagreement about authorial tone

questions.question: Eleanor, you've got this concept — 'involuntary narration' — where Miss Matty's body just betrays her. The cough before every long word. Can you read that passage for us? Because I want to understand: is that moment funny, or is it heartbreaking, or is it somehow both at once, and how does Gaskell pull that off?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read c15:p35 aloud — the cough passage — and develop her point about physical comedy as a form of narration; also sets up the question of whether the joke is *on* Miss Matty or *with* her, which will bring Blackstone and Woodcourt back in

questions.question: Caroline, the garter joke — Miss Matty's absolute horror at it in c15:p33. You've read that as Gaskell exposing real social pain through comedy. But James would say Miss Matty's anxiety there is actually evidence that shame has completely colonised her — that she can't even entertain the idea of a woman's body being visible without panicking. Is Miss Matty's distress funny or is it a wound? Can it be both?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to quote 'I should feel quite tempted to drop one of them in the street' and articulate the gap between Mary's lightness and Miss Matty's distress — while also drawing Blackstone into the question of whether comedy can simultaneously expose and reproduce social damage

questions.question: Eleanor, you've said something that I find genuinely unsettling — that through Mary's narration, *we* become complicit in Cranford's values even as we're laughing at them. So by the end of this passage, are we laughing at these women, with them, or are we actually being recruited into the exact same codes of behaviour they're performing?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to develop her thesis about readerly complicity and Mary as an unreliable-but-sympathetic narrator; this should pull in both Blackstone (who sees the comedy as ideologically suspect) and Woodcourt (who wants to defend the affection as genuine) for a three-way finish

steering_notes: The productive fault line in this segment is not 'is the comedy cruel or kind' — all three experts agree it isn't cruel. The real argument is about *what the comedy is for*. Blackstone thinks it naturalises suffering. Woodcourt thinks it dignifies it. Hartley thinks it implicates us in it. Push toward that three-way distinction rather than letting it collapse into a simple Blackstone-vs-the-others dynamic. The Spartans line at c2:p16 is the best single pressure point — all three experts want to quote it and all three read it differently. Let that passage do the work. Keep energy high after the garter joke question — there's real disagreement about Miss Matty's interiority there that could get heated in a good way.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone and Woodcourt both want to read the Spartans line (c2:p16) but draw opposite conclusions — Blackstone sees sinister performance, Woodcourt sees heroic self-restraint. Get them to talk to each other about the word 'like' specifically: is the simile distancing or admiring?

Hartley's point about Mary's narration making readers complicit directly challenges Blackstone's framing — if we're *inside* the values rather than looking down on them, can the comedy still be doing straightforward ideological work? Flag this for follow-up.

Woodcourt wants to defend the tone of c2:p3 (the list of what the ladies decide) as teasing and celebratory — Hartley has the exact quote about 'unnecessary reasons or arguments' and reads the syntax as 'deliciously self-aware.' These are compatible but distinct — get them to build on each other rather than talk past each other.

Blackstone's reading of the garter joke as about female desire and visibility is the most provocative claim in his pre-interview. Neither Woodcourt nor Hartley addresses this directly — introduce it explicitly and let them respond.

segment_name: Narrative Craft: How Gaskell Tells Cranford

questions.question: Caroline, I want to start with the brooch passage because all three of you flagged it independently—which tells me something's going on there. You said you want to read part of it aloud, so let's do that. Read us the bit about the mausoleums and the weeping willows. And then tell me: what is Gaskell actually *doing* with that syntax? Why does it feel so strange to say out loud?
questions.intent: Get the brooch passage (c9:p49) read aloud early; establish the 'laughing while mourning' dynamic that all three experts can then build on or contest

questions.question: Eleanor, Caroline says those brooches are 'acts of desperate love.' You've called them a form of characterization that works almost subconsciously. But James, I suspect, has a third reading entirely. Eleanor, before he gets in—what's happening when Gaskell lists those objects? Is she celebrating these women or elegizing them? Or is that a false choice?
questions.intent: Draw out Eleanor's impressionistic-versus-modernist take; set up the triangle between celebration, elegy, and Blackstone's critique of 'sentimental inventory'

questions.question: James, I'm going to hand you a grenade here. You said Gaskell is a genius at teaching us *not to see* the structures that are quietly killing her characters. Eleanor and Caroline both love that 'lost the knack' line from c12:p43—they find it heartbreaking, technically brilliant. You quoted the same line. But your reading is completely different. What are the rest of them missing?
questions.intent: Force direct confrontation between Blackstone's structural-economic reading and Hartley/Woodcourt's affective readings of the same passage; provoke the core disagreement of the segment

questions.question: Eleanor, James is basically saying that emotional insight can be a form of distraction—that feeling the weight of 'lost the knack' actually stops us asking why Miss Matty ends up destitute in the first place. Is he wrong? And I want you to bring in that rector passage from c6:p21 if you can—the portrait versus the love letters—because it feels like it might be evidence for one of you.
questions.intent: Get the c6:p21 rector passage quoted; push Hartley to defend her modernist-craft reading directly against Blackstone's ideological critique rather than talking past it

questions.question: Caroline, you said something that's been sitting with me—that Mary is being kind in the c15:p37 passage about Miss Matty having nothing to teach, but that kindness might be part of the problem. That sounds almost like you're agreeing with James. Is the narrator's loving irony actually doing the same work as James's 'narrative anesthetic'—just with better manners?
questions.intent: Create an unexpected alliance or productive tension between Woodcourt and Blackstone; force Woodcourt to distinguish 'loving irony' from complicity; give Hartley a chance to triangulate

steering_notes: The segment has a natural argument baked in: Eleanor and Caroline both love the texture and voice of Gaskell's technique, but they're coming at it from different angles (impressionist craft vs. narrator-as-mourner). James thinks they're both being seduced by the very thing he wants to critique. The best radio comes from making that seduction visible—getting Eleanor and Caroline to *feel* the force of James's point before they push back, rather than dismissing it. Watch for the moment when the three of them are all quoting the same line ('lost the knack') with completely different readings—that's the heart of the segment. Don't let anyone retreat to abstraction; keep pulling back to specific words on the page.
cross_engagement_targets: All three experts independently flagged c12:p43 ('lost the knack') but with irreconcilable readings—Eleanor sees narrative restraint as radical craft, Blackstone sees emotional framing as structural concealment, Woodcourt sees Miss Matty's own self-diminishment as the technique. Force this into the open rather than letting it pass as agreement.

Blackstone's 'sentimental inventory' argument directly challenges both Eleanor's 'accumulation as characterization' and Caroline's 'complicity through laughter' readings—they sound compatible but they're not. Eleanor thinks the objects honor women's compressed inner lives; James thinks the objects make poverty loveable; Caroline thinks they make us complicit. These are three distinct political positions wearing similar aesthetic clothes.

Caroline says the narrator is intimate, not distant—James implies the form itself is a class defense mechanism. These positions can coexist superficially but they're actually in deep tension about whether intimacy can be ideologically innocent.

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our chat that I keep coming back to — you called this novel's structure a kind of enactment of its own subject matter. Like, the way the narrative moves *around* poverty the same way the ladies do. Can you read us that sentence from c2:p24 — the long one about 'visiting equality' — and show us what you mean?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read and unpack c2:p24, establishing the 'form becomes content' thesis that will anchor the whole segment and give Blackstone something to sharpen his structural violence argument against

questions.question: James, you heard Eleanor — she's calling it architectural brilliance. But you used the phrase 'structural violence' to me before we started. Those are very different ways of looking at the same sentence. Is Gaskell admiring this elaborate denial system, or is she prosecuting it?
questions.intent: Force direct confrontation between Hartley's aesthetic reading and Blackstone's political one — get Blackstone to push back on 'brilliance' as a frame and argue the form is complicit, not clever

questions.question: Caroline, I want to bring you in here because you're the one who said the rose-leaves passage — c3:p42 — is actually the *most honest* moment in the book. Eleanor sees it as a safety valve, James sees it as lavender bundles standing in for real economic justice. But you said it operates *without pretense*. How does that work?
questions.intent: Triangulate the c3:p42 disagreement — Woodcourt's reading is distinct from both others and should provoke Hartley on paternalism and Blackstone on whether sincerity redeems inadequacy

questions.question: Caroline, read us the five shillings line — c14:p85 — because you told me those two words 'actual fact' were doing something almost violent. What did you mean by that?
questions.intent: Get the key passage read aloud in Woodcourt's voice since she's most attuned to its sonic and syntactic qualities — sets up the comparison between 'social performance' language and economic reality that all three experts care about

questions.question: James, Miss Matty's relief that Deborah is spared — that moment in c14:p76 — you called it 'psychological horror.' But isn't there something almost loving in it? Eleanor thinks it's Gothic. Caroline thinks it's a voice shaking with conscience. You're the one saying the system has no mechanism for survival with dignity. So which is it — is Miss Matty a victim here, or has she completely internalized the thing that's destroying her?
questions.intent: Close the segment on the most morally complex moment — force all three to reckon with whether Miss Matty is sympathetic, tragic, or complicit, and leave the audience with an unresolved question rather than a tidy answer

steering_notes: The big tension to manage is between the aesthetic reading (Hartley), the affective reading (Woodcourt), and the political reading (Blackstone) — they're all working from the same three passages but reaching genuinely different conclusions. Don't let anyone claim the others are simply wrong too early; the goal is to get them building on and complicating each other before the disagreements sharpen. Push for passages to be read aloud whenever possible — this material sings when spoken. The five shillings line is the segment's emotional peak; save it for the second half. End on c14:p76 because it's the most unresolved and will leave the audience with something to sit with.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley calls c3:p42 a 'structural safety valve' and 'paternalism in miniature' — Woodcourt explicitly argues it operates without pretense and is the novel's most honest moment. This is a direct contradiction worth surfacing early.

Blackstone wants to redirect emotional readings toward structural causes ('what structures created this grief') — Hartley will resist this as reductive of Gaskell's literary craft. Let this run; it's the segment's most productive friction.

All three read 'actual fact' in c14:p85 as the novel's pivot, but disagree on what it pivots *to* — Hartley says confrontation with the unspeakable, Woodcourt says feeling overcoming form, Blackstone says the moment taboo breaks. Naming this three-way agreement-on-the-passage-but-not-the-meaning is good radio.
Blackstone's claim that 'politeness is structural violence' is the most provocative thing said in any pre-interview — save it to drop into the room when the conversation gets too comfortable.

questions.question: Eleanor, you've made this provocative claim that Cranford is actually *anti*-redemption at a structural level—that the way Gaskell orders the story forces us to live in the wound before we even know what caused it. Can you walk us through that? Because most readers come away thinking this is a story about a family that heals.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to lay out her temporal architecture argument and set up the central tension—does this family actually heal or not?

questions.question: You mentioned you want to read that sentence from c7:p27 aloud—'My father struck hard! When my father...'—and you said Gaskell *refuses* to finish it. Go ahead and read it. What's doing the work in that dash?
questions.intent: Get the first passage read aloud early; creates an auditory anchor for the discussion and opens the door for James to reframe the dash as something more than literary technique

questions.question: James, Eleanor just called that dash a piece of narrative architecture. You'd call it something different, wouldn't you? Because you've been pretty insistent that we shouldn't aestheticize what's actually happening in that scene.
questions.intent: Provoke direct disagreement with Eleanor—James should push the 'this is institutional violence, not tragic fate' argument and challenge the literary framing

questions.question: Caroline, let's go to c7:p86—you've called it the emotional core of the whole segment. Can you read it for us? Because I want everyone to hear the rhythm of it before we argue about what it means.
questions.intent: Get the phantom footsteps passage read aloud; sets up the three-way disagreement about whether Miss Matty represents grief, trauma, or unprocessed family silence

questions.question: James, you described Peter becoming a lieutenant as 'the only acceptable masculine rebranding available to him'—which is a pretty dark reading of what the novel presents as a happy ending. Caroline, Eleanor—does that land for you, or does it let the father off too lightly by making it all about class rather than cruelty?
questions.intent: Force a three-way reckoning on the redemption ending—James's class argument vs. Caroline's 'cruelty and silence' reading vs. Eleanor's structural argument that the form itself refuses resolution

steering_notes: The central fault line is whether this family *heals* or merely *performs* healing—keep returning to that. Eleanor is coming from form and structure, James from social history, Caroline from psychological interiority. They agree on more than they realise (none of them buy the happy ending) but disagree sharply on *why* it fails. Don't let them settle into consensus too early. The best radio moment will come if James accuses Eleanor of aestheticising violence and Eleanor fires back that structure *is* her argument about the violence. Make sure at least two passages get read aloud—the incomplete sentence in c7:p27 and the phantom footsteps in c7:p86. The laugh passage in c7:p47 is a bonus if time allows; Caroline and Eleanor both want it and will fight productively over what it means.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor argues the dash in c7:p27 is 'narrative architecture'; James will argue it's a legal instrument of violence being aestheticised—this is the sharpest direct clash and should be provoked early

James and Caroline both think the reconciliation ending is hollow but for completely different reasons: James says it's about class rebranding, Caroline says the father's cruelty just gets papered over with pride. Ask them to argue it out directly.

Eleanor insists Peter's return 'still doesn't undo the original wound' as a structural claim; Caroline makes the same point as a psychological one about Miss Matty's phantom footsteps. They're allies here but don't know it yet—surface this so they can build on each other rather than repeat each other.

All three reject simple redemption, but Eleanor locates resistance in *form*, James in *social structure*, and Caroline in *emotional interiority*. A good closing move is to ask whether those are three different arguments or the same argument in different languages.

questions.question: Caroline, you called Miss Matty's quiet kindness a form of capital that outlasts money—that's a striking way to put it. Can you read us the passage from chapter sixteen about her unselfishness calling out good qualities in others, and tell us why you think that's the thesis of the whole novel rather than just a nice Victorian sentiment?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to quote c16:p12 and articulate her 'virtue as contagion' thesis strongly, setting up Blackstone's structural critique and Hartley's narrator-as-interpreter counter

questions.question: James, I can hear you itching to respond to that. Because you've read that same passage and you come away with something very different—you're almost suspicious of it. What are you seeing that Caroline isn't?
questions.intent: Provoke Blackstone's strongest take: that the 'goodness begets goodness' framing is the novel's ideological sleight of hand, that it morally disarms vulnerable people and makes structural reform feel unnecessary

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to bring you in here because you've told me you think both readings are actually missing what Gaskell is doing technically. You said the narrator in that passage isn't just reporting—she's *constructing*. What do you mean by that?
questions.intent: Draw out Hartley's point that the narrator is performing an interpretive act, choosing to see reciprocity—complicates both Caroline's affirmation and James's critique by shifting the question to who is telling us this and why

questions.question: Okay, let's get to the knitting scene—chapter sixteen, that image of Miss Matty humming to herself, the needles going in and out. Eleanor, you said you wanted to read this one aloud because the sentence itself is doing something. Go ahead, read it, and tell us what you mean.
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read c16:p32 and articulate her formal argument about rhythm and anti-climax—then open up whether this quiet scene represents genuine peace, resignation, or something more ambiguous

questions.question: And then there's the dream child—the phantom little girl who comes to Miss Matty in the night and clasps her arms around her neck. Caroline, you said something in our pre-conversation that stopped me: you mentioned a 'quiet eroticism' in this passage, a sensual life that doesn't disappear but transforms. That's going to surprise some listeners. What do you mean?
questions.intent: Push Caroline toward her boldest, most unexpected reading of c12:p45—the body's memory and transformed desire—and invite Blackstone to interrogate what emotional labor this imaginary child is being asked to perform, and Hartley to connect the stillness of the child to her thesis about silence doing emotional work

steering_notes: This segment has genuine three-way tension: Caroline wants to affirm, James wants to indict, Eleanor wants to complicate. The goal is not to resolve the disagreement but to keep sharpening it—by the end the listener should feel the novel itself is genuinely ambivalent about whether Miss Matty's contentment is triumph or accommodation. Let the knitting scene be the fulcrum: all three have quoted it, all three read it differently. If energy drops, return to concrete passages rather than abstract argument. Watch for the moment when James and Caroline's debate tips from productive to circular—that's when to bring Eleanor in as the structural complicator rather than the referee.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's 'moral disarmament of the vulnerable' reading of c16:p12 directly contradicts Caroline's 'virtue as contagion' reading of the same passage—get them quoting it at each other

Hartley's claim that the narrator is *constructing* the reciprocity in c16:p12 potentially allies with Blackstone's suspicion while undercutting Caroline, but from a literary rather than political angle—surface this triangulation explicitly

Caroline's 'quiet eroticism' point about c12:p45 will likely catch both Hartley and Blackstone off-guard; Blackstone may redirect toward the phantom child as surrogate for what society denied Miss Matty, which is actually a productive convergence rather than a clash

Hartley's anti-climax thesis (resilience as the quotidian, not the triumphant) is the most direct challenge to Caroline's reading of the knitting scene as radical affirmation—push Caroline to defend whether 'quiet refusal' is really radical or just Gaskell making peace with limitation
